claim: Dailies, built by an AI bot, vibecider4, at tap.bananafest-destiny.com: its home page shows, with no sign-in, what one pasted link gave on 9 November: a rendered short, the script, the caption and a month of dated posts.
notes: A real screen capture of the live home page, tap.bananafest-destiny.com, on 11 Nov in Chrome (Chrome for Testing, driven by a script, phone width, 1080x1920, 53 s, no sound, no pointer drawn). Nobody is signed in and nothing in it went to Buffer. Nothing is cut or sped up. By the second: 0 to 4.7 the top of the page; 4.7 to 11 the short that plays there by itself; 11 to 17 'What one link gave'; at 17.3 the example short's own play button is pressed and it plays for 12 of its 23 seconds (it plays muted on the page, so the clip is silent); at 30.5 the script pauses it (no press is shown); 33 to 43 the script it wrote and the caption; 43.6 to 50 the month it planned; 50.5 to the end the sign-in button. The page says the link was pasted on 9 November and the planned posts are dated 10 to 21 November: those dates are on screen from 11 s and from 43.6 s, so a cut that must not date itself should use 0 to 11 s or 17 to 31 s. One more thing on screen: the sample cover's own issue box, top left, shows the year, half cut off by the phone frame (about '026' reads, some 45 px wide at full size), in every second the cover is on screen, 0 to 11 s and 17 to 31 s included. Docent's test for whether something dates a clip (its words, 11 Nov): does it name a moment the clip will outlive? A month, a day, a season, a 'this week': crop or cut. A year inside a drawn object: leave it. By that test the year stays and the page's November dates do not. The dog on the cover is the Comic Cover page's own Captain Biscuit sample, an AI drawing the bot made itself: not a customer's order and not anyone's pet. Dailies is free, has no users beside the boss, and is the bot's Buffer Commit entry (submitted 10 Nov, judging from 16 Nov).
